title: The Big Bang
objective: After this level you can explain what the Big Bang theory says and what it doesn’t.
summary: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, hot and dense, and has expanded and cooled ever since. It wasn’t an explosion in space.

cards.headline: Everything you’ve met in this course began hot and dense.
cards.body: Level 88 showed galaxies moving apart. So run the movie backwards. Where does it lead?

cards.headline: Rewind the expansion
cards.body: If galaxies are drifting apart today, they were closer together yesterday. Keep rewinding and everything crowds closer, hotter and denser. The Big Bang theory says the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since. So the universe has a birthday, and everything since has been one very long cool-down.
cards.callout: Hot and dense → expanding and cooling

cards.headline: Not an explosion
cards.body: Forget the fireworks. The Big Bang was not an explosion flinging stuff into empty space. It was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. No center, no blast site, no seat with the best view. The twist: the name came in 1949 from astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favored a rival theory. The most famous name in cosmology was coined by the other team.

mascot.line: People picture a blast in empty space. Picture space itself stretching, everywhere at once.

cards.headline: The first ingredients
cards.body: In its first few minutes, the young universe made its starter kit: hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium. That’s it. Nearly every heavier element, from the carbon in you to the iron in a frying pan, would be made later, inside stars. And what came before the Big Bang, if anything? The theory doesn’t say. It tells the story of the cool-down, not what came before the first page.

cards.headline: The Big Bang: understood
learned: The universe began ~13.8 billion years ago, hot and dense
It has been expanding and cooling ever since
The Big Bang was space expanding, not an explosion
The first minutes made hydrogen and helium

questions.prompt: According to the Big Bang theory, how did the universe begin?

options.label: As a cold, empty void that slowly heated up
In an extremely hot, dense state, then expanded
As a single giant star that later exploded
options.rationale: There were no stars at the start.

options.label: As a swarm of galaxies moving inward

questions.explanation: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, extremely hot and dense, and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off in space?

options.label: Space itself expanded, everywhere at once
There was no matter until much later
options.rationale: Hydrogen and helium formed within minutes.

options.label: It happened at the center of the Milky Way
Bombs are much hotter than the Big Bang was
options.rationale: The early universe was extremely hot.

questions.explanation: A bomb explodes into space that already exists. The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself, with no center.

questions.prompt: From Level 32: stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Where did those elements first come from?

options.label: The first minutes after the Big Bang

questions.explanation: Hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium, formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
